current_activity: Le Havre: attacks from the north-east with the 34th Tank Brigade after the last heavy raid, to take the north plateau
notes: Event date: 10 September 1944, 17:30 (Ellis, vol. II, pp. 7, 14). Event definition: I Corps begins the assault on Le Havre almost as soon as the last heavy bomber raid ends at 17:30 on 10 September; the 49th Division, with the 34th Tank Brigade under command, sets out from the north-east to capture the defences of the north plateau and then to cross the Fontaine valley to the south plateau; the 51st Division joins on its right at midnight; the division had closed round the perimeter with the 51st Division on 4 September (pp. 7 and 14). Event support: one source family (Ellis, the British official history). Ellis, Victory in the West, vol. II, p. 7: "On the 4th the two divisions closed round the perimeter"; p. 14: "Almost as soon as the last heavy bomber attack finished at 5.30 in the afternoon of the roth, an attack by I Corps began which was to continue through the night"; "The 49th Division, with the 34th Tank Brigade under command, set out from the north-east to capture the defences of the north plateau". Location: Le Havre, France (existing place PL0169) with a precision of 5 km. Location approximate: the point is the town of Le Havre, the objective; the attack came from the north-east and the division headquarters is not named. Location support: Ellis names Le Havre as the objective (p. 14); the attack comes from the north-east. Review (British Batch 2, 28 October 2026; inferred value; old value: operation_id OP-CAMP-NORTHERN-FRANCE; new value: operation_id OP-ASTONIA): the row is part of the I Corps assault on Le Havre of 10 to 12 September 1944, which Stacey, p. 331, calls a neat and expeditious three-day operation in the second week of September and names Operation Astonia; the new operation is a child of OP-CAMP-NORTHERN-FRANCE, so the narrower operation replaces the broader one. The other rows under OP-CAMP-NORTHERN-FRANCE are not about Le Havre. current_activity: Nijmegen Island flooded after dykes blown; repulses a local attack on 4 December; commands the Island from the 6th
notes: Event date: 4 December 1944 (Stacey, p. 433). Event definition: The enemy blows dykes north of Elst and west of Arnhem and floods the Island (the 49th Division reports the dykes blown north of Elst on 2 December); in conjunction with the flooding the enemy puts in a local attack against the division on 4 December, which is sharply repulsed; the situation settles down with units of both the 49th and the 51st (Highland) Division keeping footholds on the Island, all under Headquarters 49th Division from the morning of the 6th, and both divisional headquarters move south of the Waal by noon on 7 December; the division is in II Canadian Corps, which took over the bridgehead on 9 November, in place of the 50th Division from the end of November (Stacey, pp. 430, 433). Event support: one source family (Stacey, the Canadian official history). Stacey, The Victory Campaign, p. 430: "places were taken by the 49th (West Riding) and 51st (Highland) Divisions"; p. 430: "were also withdrawn into reserve, at the end of November"; p. 433: "The emergency came the very next day, when the 49th Division reported dykes blown north of Elst and west of Arnhem"; p. 433: "the enemy put in a local attack against the 49th Division on 4 December. It was sharply repulsed"; p. 433: "under Headquarters 49th Division from the morning of the 6th". Location: Elst, Gelderland (new place, see the 50th Division row of 1 October 1944), the village north of which the dykes were blown with a precision of 10 km. Location approximate: the point is the village of Elst, near the middle of the Island between the Waal and the Lower Rhine; the sector of the division and its headquarters are not named. Location support: Stacey names Elst as the place north of which the dykes were blown and puts the division on the Island (pp. 433, 430). Commander: Maj.-Gen. G. H. A. MacMillan, who succeeded Maj.-Gen. E. H. Barker (to 29.11.44) in command of the 49th Division and held it to 24.3.45 (Ellis, vol. II, p. 376). Context: Review (British Batch 2 follow-up, 28 October 2026): the row gives the division a parent for the winter of 1944-45 (II Canadian Corps, attached) and replaces nothing; the single Ellis row of 18 January 1945 at Zetten (C1482) keeps its empty parent field because Ellis does not name the corps, but the attachment relation covers its date. current_activity: Nijmegen bridgehead: German 6th Parachute Division attacks near Zetten; positions regained by the evening of the 21st
notes: Event date: 18 January 1945, shortly before daylight (Ellis, vol. II, pp. 240, 241). Event definition: Shortly before daylight on 18 January the German 6th Parachute Division attacks the division near Zetten, about nine miles south-west of Arnhem, in an area the division occupied when the floods began to subside at the end of December; some outposts are overrun and a confused fight lasts the rest of the day; the Germans attack again next morning, the division counter-attacks and regains most of Zetten, and by the evening of the 21st the original positions are re-established; the Germans lose 340 prisoners and, by British calculation, another 470 killed and wounded, and the division and supporting troops have 220 casualties (p. 240). Event support: one source family (Ellis, the British official history). Ellis, Victory in the West, vol. II, pp. 240-241: "Shortly before daylight on the 18th of January the German 6th Parachute Division opened another attack on the 49th Division"; "This time it was near Zetten, about nine miles south-west of Arnhem, an area occupied by the 49th Division when the floods began to subside at the end of December"; "by the evening of the 21st our original positions were re-established". Location: Zetten, Gelderland (new place), the village at the centre of the fight with a precision of 3 km. Location approximate: the point is Zetten, the village fought for; the division held the surrounding area of the Nijmegen bridgehead and its headquarters is not named. Location support: Ellis names Zetten and the area the division held (p. 240). Context: The page does not name the corps over the division on 18 January 1945; Ellis, vol. II, p. 256 (note) puts the division in II Canadian Corps when Veritable opened on 8 February, three weeks later, so parent_unit_id is left empty (inferred: not set). Review (British Batch 2 follow-up, 28 October 2026): the row is unchanged; two links to command relations were added. The old value is: no relation listed (parent_unit_id empty). The new value is: the row lists the standing assignment to I Corps (CR0888) and the temporary attachment to II Canadian Corps (CR0920), both as observed_during. The reason is that Stacey, pp. 430 and 433, put the 49th Division on the Nijmegen Island under II Canadian Corps from the end of November 1944, and the row (Zetten, 18 January 1945) shows the division still there; the Ellis page behind the row names no corps, so the parent_unit_id field stays empty.
